newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM TO TWEEK STRUCTURE OF 10 TRILLION BFR DEBT.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM TO TWEEK STRUCTURE OF 10 TRILLION BFR DEBT.

text.p: Belgium will fine-tune the structure of its 10,000 billion Belgian franc debt, following an 18-month study into how to minimise its cost, Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said on Wednesday.
"I think we can say the results up to now are relatively good, although it has shown us we have to change certain aspects," Maystadt told a parliamentary finance committee meeting.

In a statement given to committee members, the Treasury said the study had shown the present structure of the debt more or less guaranteed new government borrowing would be kept in the coming years below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), as required under a single European currency.

"One of the major conclusions is that...the probability of meeting the budgetary objectives, by simply maintaining the existing structure of the debt and the level of primary surplus, is more than 90 percent," the Treasury said in a statement.
Belgium's government, which actually has a positive balance between spending and revenues, is consistently in the red because of the cost of servicing the national debt.
The study compared Belgium's actual debt against a theoretical "benchmark debt portfolio" developed by the Treasury with advice from banks UBS and Morgan Stanley.
The benchmark was tested under four scenarios to see if the government could keep its borrowing costs within preset limits.

The scenarios were: European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) happens on time with Belgium among its members; EMU starting on time, but after a period of market volatility; EMU being postponed to a later or imprecise date; and EMU starting on time but without Belgium, with Belgium's entry anticipated in a second wave.

"One of the major conclusions of the analysis is that the actual structure of the public debt is reasonably close to (the benchmark goals) and has an adequate cost/risk ratio," the Treasury said in its written statement.

Treasury adviser Louis de Montpellier told the committee that only in the last scenario was the present structure likely to prove inadequate. "In this case we would be at the limit of meeting our objectives, with a 65 percent chance," he said.
Belgium's debt is presently held mainly in Belgian francs, or other "hard core" European currencies. Only five percent is held in other currencies such as the dollar, yen or Swiss franc, he noted.

Maystadt did not indicate in which way the debt would be fine tuned. He said however it would not be a one-off process, but that having the new benchmark portfolio allowed the Treasury to constantly optimise its debt management.
The Treasury has scheduled a news conference on Thursday to present more details of the benchmark system to the press.
